anchor: Floating Rate Bonds (FRBs) and Government securities
argumentsAgainst: The floating coupon improves alignment with prevailing short-term government borrowing yields, but it also makes future interest payments less predictable for investors.
The source establishes the reset formula and current rate, but does not establish FRB 2034’s maturity structure, investor base, market liquidity or fiscal-cost implications.
argumentsFor: A formula linked to recent 182-day T-Bill yields creates a transparent and pre-announced basis for periodic coupon resetting.
The fixed spread of 0.98 percentage point provides an additional return over the specified base rate.
background: The Reserve Bank of India’s FAQ describes Floating Rate Bonds as securities whose coupon is variable and reset at pre-announced intervals; it describes Treasury bills as short-term Government of India debt instruments issued at a discount a
The RBI FAQ identifies 182-day Treasury bills as one of the Government of India’s T-Bill tenors and states that RBI conducts T-Bill auctions.[8]
indiaImplications: For public debt management, linking the coupon to recent 182-day T-Bill yields can make the instrument responsive to short-term market conditions; the source does not quantify its effect on borrowing costs.
For investors, the reset mechanism may reduce the risk of being locked into an unchanged coupon when the linked short-term yield changes, while introducing variability in future income.

For monetary and financial-market analysis, the instrument illustrates how sovereign borrowing instruments can transmit movements in short-term government-security yields into periodic interest payments.

mainsPractice.stem: Discuss how the coupon-setting mechanism of Government of India Floating Rate Bond 2034 reflects the trade-off between transparency, flexibility and interest-rate certainty.

officialFacts.text: The rate of interest on Government of India Floating Rate Bond 2034 (FRB 2034) applicable for the half year October 30, 2026 to April 29, 2027 shall be 7.26 per cent per annum.

FRB 2034 carries a coupon, which has a base rate equivalent to the average of the Weighted Average Yield (WAY) of last three auctions (from the rate fixing day i.e., October 30, 2026) of 182 Day T-Bills, plus a fixed spread (0.98 per cent).

sections.heading: RBI announcement and mechanism
paragraphs: On October 29, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India announced that the interest rate on Government of India Floating Rate Bond 2034 would be 7.26% per annum for October 30, 2026 to April 29, 2027. The coupon’s base is the average Weighted Average Yield of the last three 182-day T-Bill auctions counted from the rate-fixing day, October 30, 2026; a fixed 0.98% spread is then added.

The mechanism therefore connects the bond’s periodic coupon to recent short-term government borrowing yields. Its practical consequence is that the coupon can respond at reset dates to the linked market rate, rather than remaining permanently fixed. A limitation is that the source does not state how the rate will change in future reset periods.

sections.heading: Why the distinction matters
paragraphs: The arrangement should not be confused with a permanently fixed-coupon bond: the source expressly describes a floating coupon formula. Nor does the announcement say that the bond’s rate equals a single 182-day T-Bill yield; it specifies an average of the last three relevant auction WAYs plus the spread.

For public-debt analysis, the formula offers an identifiable reference and a known margin, supporting transparency in coupon determination. For investors, the same reset feature can mean changing future income. The RBI’s FAQ separately describes T-bills as short-term, zero-coupon instruments issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, while describing FRBs as securities whose coupons reset at pre-announced intervals.[8]

advisory_notes: The proposed codes GS3.1 and GS3.2 are not an official UPSC syllabus numbering system; map the topic to GS-III economic development, public finance and government budgeting more explicitly.
The phrase “longer-dated sovereign instrument” is analytical framing and is not established by the supplied announcement, which does not state FRB 2034’s maturity.
“Interest-rate transmission” is a reasonable analytical use, but the announcement itself establishes only the coupon formula and rate, not a transmission effect.
“Investor protection” may overstate the implication; the pre-announced formula improves transparency, but protection outcomes are not demonstrated by the source.
“Government borrowing yields” should be narrowed to the specified 182-day T-bill auction yields; the source does not establish broader borrowing-yield effects.
“Periodic interest payments” and “future income” are reasonable implications of a coupon-bearing FRB, but the supplied extract does not independently provide the full payment structure.
The hypothetical using X is correctly labelled as an illustration and does not assert an unsupported numerical value.
The applied-question answer accurately reproduces the stated formula and announced rate, but calling it a “half-year rate” is less precise than “rate applicable for the half-year.”

wayForward: Maintain clear, pre-announced reference rates and reset dates so investors can independently understand coupon determination.
Monitor the effect of floating-rate borrowing on future debt-servicing uncertainty as linked short-term yields change.
Present the fixed spread separately from the reference yield to preserve transparency in public-debt communication.
